a: In many pieces and in many ways
t: A sentence that opens with five p's
p: The Greek opens with a run of p-sounds, the first sign of how carefully Hebrews is written.
b: The opening words are polymerōs kai polytropōs, 'in many parts and in many manners'. The first sentence of the Greek has five words that begin with p: polymerōs, polytropōs, palai ('long ago'), patrasin ('fathers') and prophētais ('prophets'). English cannot keep the sound, so the Plain keeps the meaning: God spoke a piece at a time, through visions, laws, songs and stories. The point is not that the old word was poor but that it was partial. Verses 1-4 are one long, balanced sentence in Greek; Origen already judged its Greek 'purer' than Paul's (Eusebius, Church History 6.25.11), and scholars of Greek often rank it the most polished in the New Testament. See the chapter page on the prologue.

p: The Greek says God spoke 'in' the prophets, not only through them.
b: The preposition is en, 'in'. Most English versions turn it into 'by' or 'through', which is the sense. But the same preposition comes back in 1:2, 'in a Son', so the Plain keeps 'in' both times: God spoke in the prophets, and now he has spoken in a Son. The pairing sets up the whole letter. The prophets carried God's word; the Son is himself the place where God speaks. 'The prophets' here means more than the books called Prophets: Moses, David and the Psalms are all quoted as God speaking.

a: At the end of these days
p: A Hebrew-flavored phrase: the final stretch of history has arrived with the Son.
b: Literally 'at the last of these days'. The Greek Old Testament uses 'the last days' for the time when God will act at last (Numbers 24:14; Isaiah 2:2; Daniel 10:14). Hebrews says that time is already here: God 'has spoken' in the Son. The same conviction is in Acts 2:17 and 1 Corinthians 10:11. Hebrews will speak later of Christ appearing 'at the completion of the ages' (9:26). The readers live in the overlap: the end has begun, but 'the world to come' (2:5) is not yet fully seen.
orig: ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάτου τῶν ἡμερῶν τούτων (ep' eschatou tōn hēmerōn toutōn)

p: The Greek has no article and no 'his': the stress falls on what kind of messenger this is.
b: Greek en huiō is simply 'in Son'. Most English Bibles add 'his', which is true, but the bare noun says something more: God's last word came in one who is a Son, not a servant like the prophets or a messenger like the angels. The whole of chapter 1 unpacks that word 'Son' with seven quotations. The title is at the heart of Hebrews' teaching about Jesus (1:5; 3:6; 4:14; 5:5, 8; 7:3, 28).

p: Psalm 2, quoted in 1:5, promised the king the nations as an inheritance.
b: Psalm 2, which 1:5 quotes, goes on: "Ask it of me, and I will hand you the nations to inherit" (Psalm 2:8). Hebrews widens the inheritance from the nations to 'all things'. The language of inheritance runs through the book: the Son inherits a name (1:4), believers 'inherit salvation' (1:14) and the promises (6:12, 17). An heir is a son, so the image fits the title.

p: Greek aiōnas means 'ages'; the KJV has 'worlds'. Both senses are in the word.
b: Aiōn usually means an age, a long span of time, as in 'the age to come' (6:5). In Jewish Greek it can also mean the world as the arena of those ages, and 11:3 uses it the same way ('the ages were set in order by a word from God'). The KJV's 'worlds' takes that sense. The Plain keeps 'the ages' so the reader can see that the Son is Lord of history as well as of the created universe. Compare John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16, where all things were made through him.

a: the brightness that shines out from God's glory
p: Greek apaugasma is light shining out from a source, or light shining back. Wisdom 7:26 uses it.
b: Apaugasma can mean the beam that shines out of a light, or the glow that shines back from it. Athanasius took the first: the Son shines out from the Father as light from its source, never apart from it. The word appears once more in the Greek Bible, in the Wisdom of Solomon, where wisdom is 'a radiance of eternal light' (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, apaugasma phōtos aidiou). Hebrews borrows Jewish language about God's Wisdom for the Son. He argued from this verse against Arius that there was never a time when the Son was not, since no one ever saw light without its radiance.

a: the exact stamp of his being
p: A charaktēr is the mark a seal or die leaves; hypostasis here means God's very being.
b: Charaktēr is the impression a die makes on a coin or a seal on wax: the exact likeness of the original. Hypostasis means what stands under, the reality or substance of a thing. Here it is God's very being (KJV 'person', from the later church use of the word). Hebrews uses the same word in two other senses: 'confidence' at 3:14 and 'assurance' at 11:1. The Plain gives a different English in each place, with a note. In the creeds of the 300s and 400s hypostasis became the technical word for each 'person' of the Trinity, which is why older translations used 'person' here.
orig: χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ (charaktēr tēs hypostaseōs autou)

p: The verb pheron means 'carrying, bearing along', moving creation toward its goal.
b: Pherōn is the ordinary word for carrying. The picture is not Atlas holding the world still on his shoulders but someone carrying all things along, keeping them in being and moving them to where God means them to go. He does it 'by his word of power', the same speaking by which God made the world (Genesis 1; Hebrews 11:3). Colossians 1:17 says the same in other words: in him all things hold together.
orig: φέρων τε τὰ πάντα (pherōn te ta panta)

t: The priest's work in one phrase
p: Cleansing from sin was the business of the Day of Atonement. Hebrews will spend chapters 7-10 on it.
b: On the Day of Atonement the high priest made the people clean: "For on this day atonement will be made for you, to make you clean" (Leviticus 16:30). The Greek katharismos, 'cleansing', is a priest's word. Hebrews names the Son's priestly work in its very first sentence, long before it calls him 'high priest' (2:17). The order matters too: he made the cleansing, and then he sat down. A priest in the tent never sat; the sitting means the work was finished (10:11-12).

a: the right hand of the Majesty in the heights
p: The first allusion to Psalm 110:1, the psalm Hebrews builds on more than any other.
b: 'The Majesty' is a respectful way of saying 'God' (again in 8:1). Taking a seat at God's right hand comes from Psalm 110:1, quoted in full at 1:13: "Sit at my right hand" (Psalm 110:1). Its fourth verse, about a priest 'after the pattern of Melchizedek', will carry chapters 5-7. Early Christians used its first verse again and again for Jesus' exaltation (Mark 12:36; Acts 2:34-35; Romans 8:34; Ephesians 1:20; 1 Peter 3:22).
r: Psalm 110:1; Hebrews 1:13; Hebrews 8:1; Hebrews 10:12; Hebrews 12:2; Acts 2:34-35

p: Kreittōn, 'better', runs through Hebrews: a better hope, covenant, sacrifice, country, resurrection.
b: Kreittōn is Hebrews' signature word. The Plain renders it 'better' every time so the reader can follow it: the Son is better than the angels (1:4), the readers are persuaded of 'better things' (6:9), the lesser is blessed by 'the better' (7:7), a 'better hope' (7:19), a 'better covenant' (7:22; 8:6), better sacrifices (9:23), a better possession (10:34), a better country (11:16), a better resurrection (11:35), something better for us (11:40), blood that speaks better than Abel's (12:24). The comparison is never 'bad against good' but 'good against better': the old was real, the new is greater.
r: Hebrews 6:9; Hebrews 7:19; Hebrews 7:22; Hebrews 8:6; Hebrews 11:16; Hebrews 12:24

a: The name he received as his inheritance
p: Readers differ: the name 'Son', the divine name, or the title Lord.
b: Hebrews does not say which name. (1) Most commentators take it to be 'Son', since the next verse asks to which angel God ever said 'You are my son'. (2) Some see the divine name itself, given to the risen Christ as in Philippians 2:9: "gave him, as a gift, the name / that is above every name" (Philippians 2:9). (3) Others think of 'Lord' (1:10). The verb 'inherited' fits (1): an heir is a son. The 'became' does not mean he was not Son before (1:2 says the ages were made through him); it means he took his seat as Son after the cross.

a: You are my son. This day I have fathered you
p: First of seven quotations: a coronation psalm, sung over a king on the day he took the throne.
b: Psalm 2 was a coronation psalm: on the day the king was crowned, God adopted him as 'son'. The site's Psalm reads: "He said to me, "You are my son." (Psalm 2:7) and "This day I have fathered you." (Psalm 2:7). Hebrews quotes the Greek, which matches. Acts 13:33 applies the same words to Jesus' resurrection, and Hebrews 5:5 to his appointment as high priest. 'This day' is the day of enthronement. Chapter 1 strings together seven quotations (1:5, 5, 6, 7, 8-9, 10-12, 13), a chain scholars call a catena, each showing what God says to the Son and never said to an angel.

a: I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me
p: From God's promise to David about his son: one of the roots of Jewish hope for a Messiah.
b: The words come from Nathan's message to David about the son who would build God's house: "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me." (2 Samuel 7:14), repeated in 1 Chronicles 17:13. Solomon was the first son meant, but the promise of a throne 'forever' (2 Samuel 7:13, 16) kept Jewish hope looking for a later son of David. The same promise speaks of a 'house', which Hebrews picks up in 3:1-6.

t: When does he lead the firstborn in?
p: Three readings: at Jesus' birth, at his exaltation, or at his second coming.
b: The Greek hotan de palin eisagagē can be read 'Again, when he leads...' (introducing another quotation, as the Plain has it) or 'When he leads... in again', that is, a second time. So: (1) the incarnation, when the firstborn entered the world (Luke 2:13-14 has angels praising); (2) the exaltation, when he was brought into 'the world to come' (2:5) and enthroned, which fits the setting of 1:3-4; (3) the second coming (9:28). 'Firstborn' recalls Psalm 89:27: "I, for my part, will make him firstborn" (Psalm 89:27), a title of rank for David's heir, and Israel as God's firstborn (Exodus 4:22).
r: Psalm 89:27; Exodus 4:22; Colossians 1:15; Colossians 1:18; Romans 8:29; Hebrews 12:23

a: And let all the angels of God bow down to him
t: A line missing from the Hebrew
p: The traditional Hebrew of Deuteronomy 32:43 lacks this line. A Dead Sea Scroll and the Greek have it.
b: The quotation is from the end of the Song of Moses. The Masoretic Text of Deuteronomy 32:43 has no such line. The Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut-q (4Q44) reads 'and bow down to him, all gods', and the site's Deuteronomy follows it: "and all you gods, bow down to him!" (Deuteronomy 32:43). The Greek of Deuteronomy in Swete's edition has 'let the sons of God bow down to him' and later 'let all the angels of God be strong in him'; the copy of the Song among the Odes printed after the Psalms reads exactly Hebrews' line, 'let all the angels of God bow down to him'. Psalm 97:7 is close too: "all you gods, bow down to him!" (Psalm 97:7); its Greek has 'all his angels'. So Hebrews quotes a real Greek form of the Song.
orig: καὶ προσκυνησάτωσαν αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι θεοῦ

a: He makes his angels into winds
p: The Hebrew says God makes the winds his messengers; the Greek, which Hebrews quotes, says he makes his angels winds.
b: The site's Psalm reads: "He makes the winds into his messengers" (Psalm 104:4). Hebrew mal'akh means both 'messenger' and 'angel', and ruach both 'wind' and 'spirit'. The Greek (Psalm 103:4 in its numbering) has ho poiōn tous angelous autou pneumata, 'who makes his angels winds' (or 'spirits'). Hebrews uses that Greek to make a point: angels are changeable servants whom God turns into wind and fire as he pleases, while the Son's throne lasts 'for ever and ever' (1:8). Some translate 'spirits' here, matching 1:14 'spirits in holy service'.
orig: ὁ ποιῶν τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα

p: 'Your throne, O God' or 'God is your throne'? Both are possible Greek; the Plain reads the first.
b: Psalm 45 addresses a king of David's line (see the note on Psalm 45:6). Hebrews' Greek, ho thronos sou ho theos, can be read two ways. (1) 'Your throne, O God', an address. Murray Harris (1984) argues the Greek translators meant this. (2) 'God is your throne', that is, the Son's rule rests on God: B. F. Westcott (1892) judged this 'best', and the New World Translation of Jehovah's Witnesses reads it so. The Plain follows (1): the next lines speak to the Son ('you have loved', 'anointed you'), and 1:7-8 sets what God says about the angels against what he says to the Son. Readers of (1) still differ. Most churches see the Son called God in the full sense. Others take the title in the derived sense it had in the psalm, where, Harris argues, a king could 'exceptionally' bear a title 'not reserved exclusively for Deity'; 1:9 has the Son anointed by 'God, your God'. The variant 'his kingdom' bears on this; see the variant.
orig: ὁ θρόνος σου ὁ θεός (ho thronos sou ho theos)

p: A ruler's staff stood for his right to rule. This one is 'straight'.
b: Rhabdos is a rod or staff; a king's rod is his scepter, the sign of his power to rule and judge. The word joined to it, euthytēs, means straightness: a rule that does not bend for bribes or favorites. The site's Psalm renders the Hebrew mishor 'fairness', and the Plain follows it. Compare Psalm 2:9, where the king rules with an iron rod, and Isaiah 11:4-5, where the shoot of Jesse judges the poor with fairness.

p: The verb chriō, 'anoint', is the root of Christos, 'Christ, Anointed One'.
b: Kings and priests in Israel were anointed with oil (1 Samuel 16:13; Exodus 29:7). The Greek verb here, chriō, gives the title Christos, 'anointed', the Greek for Hebrew mashiach, 'Messiah'. Hebrews has just called the Son 'God' (1:8) and now says that 'God, your God' anointed him: the Son is both addressed as God and set apart by God. 'The oil of rejoicing' is festive oil, used at feasts and weddings (Psalm 45 is a wedding song), not only the oil of office.

p: Metochoi means 'partners, sharers'. Hebrews uses it of believers in 3:1, 14 and 6:4.
b: In the psalm the king's metochoi are his companions at court or fellow princes. Hebrews uses the same word for its readers: 'partners in a calling from heaven' (3:1), 'partners of Christ' (3:14), 'partners in the Holy Spirit' (6:4), and in 12:8 of sons who share in discipline. The Plain renders it 'partners' every time so the link shows. The Son is raised 'above' his partners, but they are his partners all the same.
orig: παρὰ τοὺς μετόχους σου (para tous metochous sou)

t: A psalm to God, read as to the Son
p: The Greek of Psalm 102 adds 'Lord', and Hebrews hears the Son addressed as Creator.
b: The site's Psalm, from the Hebrew, reads: "Long ago you set the earth on its foundations; / your hands made the heavens." (Psalm 102:25). The Hebrew has no title in that line. The Greek (Psalm 101:26) has sy, kyrie, 'you, Lord'. Since Hebrews takes 'Lord' as the Son's title, it reads the whole passage as God speaking to the Son: he laid the earth's foundations, and he stays the same when everything else wears out. This is one of the clearest places where the New Testament takes words addressed to Israel's God and applies them to Jesus.
orig: σὺ κατ᾽ ἀρχάς, κύριε (sy kat' archas, kyrie)

a: roll them up like a mantle
p: The image of the heavens rolled up like a garment or scroll also appears in Isaiah and Revelation.
b: Isaiah has the same picture of the end of the old order: "the sky will roll up like a scroll" (Isaiah 34:4). Revelation 6:14 repeats it. A peribolaion is a wrap or mantle, thrown around the shoulders and taken off again. Some early manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Claromontanus before correction) read 'you will change them' (allaxeis) instead of 'roll them up' (helixeis), a difference of a few letters. Hebrews 12:26-27 returns to the theme: what is made will be shaken and removed.

p: This line sets up Hebrews 13:8, 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today'.
b: The site's Psalm has the Hebrew 'you are he': "But you are he, / and your years will never run out." (Psalm 102:27). The Greek has ho autos, 'the same'. Hebrews will close with the same word: 'Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and for all the ages' (13:8). In a world where heaven and earth wear thin like an old coat, the Son does not change.

t: Psalm 110:1, the last of the seven
p: Jesus himself asked about this verse; Hebrews ends the chain of seven with it.
b: The Greek is the same as in Acts and Luke, and the Plain follows them: "Sit at my right hand," (Acts 2:34) "until I set your enemies down as a footstool for your feet." (Acts 2:35). In Mark 12:35-37 Jesus asked how David's son could be David's 'Lord'. Hebrews has already alluded to the verse (1:3) and will come back to it (8:1; 10:12-13; 12:2). It also leads straight into the psalm's fourth verse, the oath about Melchizedek (5:6). The waiting 'until' matters: the enemies are not yet all under his feet (2:8; 10:13).

p: Leitourgika, 'serving', is a word for worship service, the root of 'liturgy'.
b: The adjective leitourgikos belongs to temple service; in the Greek Old Testament it describes the vessels and garments of worship (Exodus 31:10; Numbers 4:12). Hebrews pictures the angels as attendants in God's heavenly sanctuary, sent out on errands for those who will inherit salvation. That is a high dignity, but it is a servant's dignity, not a son's. The idea that angels guard and help God's people runs from Psalm 91:11 to Jesus' words about the little ones whose "angels in heaven are always looking on the face of my Father in heaven" (Matthew 18:10).

p: Pararreō means to flow past or slip away: the danger is drift, not open revolt.
b: The verb pararreō is used of water flowing past, or of something slipping away unnoticed. The readers are not being warned first against open rebellion but against slowly floating away from what they heard, like a boat whose rope has worked loose. The first of Hebrews' warnings is mild, and the warnings grow sharper: 2:1-4; 3:7-4:13; 5:11-6:12; 10:26-39; 12:14-29.

p: Jewish tradition held that angels took part in giving the law at Sinai. Acts and Galatians say so too.
b: Exodus does not mention angels at Sinai, but Jewish tradition did. The Greek of Deuteronomy 33:2 says the Lord came from Sinai with 'angels with him at his right hand'. Jubilees has the angel of the presence write the law for Moses (Jubilees 1). Josephus puts in Herod's mouth the claim that the Jews learned their holiest laws 'by angels'. The New Testament assumes it: "You were given the law by the orders of angels, and you never kept it." (Acts 7:53); "It was arranged through angels, by the hand of a mediator." (Galatians 3:19). Hebrews' argument runs: if the word through angels was binding, how much more the word through the Lord.

a: every transgression and every refusal to listen
p: Parabasis is crossing a marked line; parakoē is literally 'hearing amiss', refusing to listen.
b: The two words are a pair. Parabasis, 'transgression', is stepping over a boundary God has drawn (the site's term for it, as in Romans). Parakoē comes from akouō, 'hear': it is hearing wrongly, or refusing to hear. That links with the call to 'keep our minds on what we heard' (2:1) and with Psalm 95's 'Today, if you hear his voice' (3:7). In Hebrews, sin is above all failing to listen to God when he speaks.
orig: πᾶσα παράβασις καὶ παρακοή (pasa parabasis kai parakoē)

a: those who heard him made it sure to us
p: The writer heard the good news from those who heard Jesus. Luther used this line against Paul's authorship.
b: The writer puts himself among those who received the message from eyewitnesses, not from the Lord himself. Paul insisted that he received his gospel by revelation and not from people (Galatians 1:11-12). Luther's preface to Hebrews uses this verse to argue that Paul did not write the letter, since its author 'speaks of the apostles as a disciple to whom this doctrine has come from the apostles'. Those who hold to Paul's authorship answer that Paul could include himself among the hearers out of modesty. See the book's authorship table.

p: Merismos means a distribution or division. God handed out gifts of the Spirit as he chose.
b: Merismos is 'a dividing, a portioning out'. Here it is the Spirit distributed in many gifts, 'as he wanted', which recalls Paul: the one Spirit gives to each one 'as he decides' (1 Corinthians 12:11). The same word comes back in 4:12, where the word of God cuts to the 'dividing' of soul and spirit. Signs, wonders and acts of power are the terms Acts uses for what God did through Jesus and the apostles (Acts 2:22, 43).

t: The world to come under angels?
p: In the Greek Bible the nations were placed under angels. The coming world will be under the Son.
b: Greek Deuteronomy 32:8 says God 'fixed the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God', and Daniel speaks of angelic 'princes' of Persia and Greece (Daniel 10:13, 20). In that picture, this age is run in part by angels. Hebrews says the next one is not: God did not put 'the world to come' (Greek oikoumenē, the inhabited world) under angels but under the human being of Psalm 8, fulfilled in Jesus. Jewish teaching spoke of 'this world' and 'the world to come'; Hebrews uses the same pair (6:5 'the age to come').
orig: τὴν οἰκουμένην τὴν μέλλουσαν (tēn oikoumenēn tēn mellousan)

p: Hebrews does not name the psalm's author. For this writer the human speaker matters less than God.
b: The writer certainly knew the verse came from Psalm 8. The vague 'someone, somewhere' (also 4:4, 'somewhere') is not ignorance but style: Hebrews almost never names the human authors of Scripture. It introduces quotations as God, the Son or the Holy Spirit speaking (1:5; 2:12; 3:7; 10:15). What matters is that God has said it.

a: What is a human being, that you remember him
t: Psalm 8: the glory of being human
p: Psalm 8 marvels that God cares for small human beings and gives them rule over creation.
b: The site's Psalm reads: "what is a mere mortal, that you remember him, / a son of man, that you look after him?" (Psalm 8:4). The psalm is about humanity in general, made in God's image and set over the works of God's hands (Genesis 1:26-28). Hebrews agrees, and then observes in 2:8 that this is not what we see: humanity does not rule creation. What we do see is Jesus (2:9), the one human being in whom the psalm has come true, who leads 'many sons into glory' (2:10).

t: Humanity or the Son of Man?
p: Is Psalm 8's 'son of man' every human, or Jesus' title? Readers differ.
b: (1) Many read Hebrews 2:6-9 as about humanity: the psalm's promise of rule was given to the human race, lost, and is fulfilled first in Jesus, who shares 'blood and flesh' with us (2:14). (2) Others hear Jesus' own title, 'the Son of Man' (Daniel 7:13; Mark 14:62), and read the psalm as about him from the start. Hebrews never uses 'Son of Man' as a title anywhere else, and the Greek here has no article, so the Plain keeps the psalm's lowercase 'a son of man', as the site's Psalm 8:4 does. The two readings need not exclude each other: Jesus is the true human being.

p: The Hebrew of Psalm 8 says 'a little less than God' (elohim); the Greek says 'than angels'.
b: The site's Psalm, from the Hebrew, has: "You made him only a little less than God" (Psalm 8:5). Hebrew elohim can mean God, gods or heavenly beings, and the Greek translators chose 'angels' (angelous). Hebrews needs that Greek reading, since its whole argument compares the Son with angels. Greek brachy ti can also mean either 'a little' in degree or 'for a little while' in time. The psalm meant degree; in 2:9 Hebrews applies it to Jesus, who was lower than angels for a short time, while he lived and died as a man.
orig: βραχύ τι παρ᾽ ἀγγέλους (brachy ti par' angelous)

a: not everything has been put under him yet
p: Paul uses the same psalm: Christ's rule has begun but is not complete.
b: Paul quotes the same line: "For "he put all things under his feet."" (1 Corinthians 15:27), and Ephesians says "God placed all things beneath his feet" (Ephesians 1:22). Hebrews is honest about the gap: right now we do not see everything under him. This is the same 'until' as in Psalm 110:1 (1:13; 10:13). The readers, who had lost property and freedom (10:32-34), needed to hear that the world as they saw it was not the end of the story.

a: because of the death he suffered
t: Crowned because he died, or lowered so that he could die?
p: The Greek phrase 'because of the suffering of death' can go with 'crowned' or with 'set below the angels'.
b: The Greek runs, word for word: 'the one set a little below angels we see, Jesus, because of the suffering of death with glory and honor crowned'. The phrase dia to pathēma tou thanatou stands between the two halves. (1) It goes with 'crowned': he is crowned because he suffered death, as in Philippians 2:8-9. The ASV, the BSB and the Plain read it this way. (2) It goes with 'set below the angels': he was made lower for the suffering of death, that is, in order to die. The KJV's punctuation reads it this way. Dia with this case usually gives a cause ('because of'), which favors (1); the next clause ('so that... he would taste death') then gives the purpose. The Greek perfect 'has been crowned' describes a lasting state; the Plain keeps it.
orig: διὰ τὸ πάθημα τοῦ θανάτου (dia to pathēma tou thanatou)

p: A Jewish idiom for going through death itself, not just touching it.
b: 'Taste death' means to experience death fully. Jesus uses it in the Gospels: "some who will never taste death before they see the kingdom of God arrived in power" (Mark 9:1). Hebrews is saying that Jesus really died, and that his death was 'on behalf of everyone'. It does not mean he only sampled death; 2:14 says he died in order to take away death's power.

p: Churches that teach Christ died for all read this plainly; the Canons of Dort read the scope of his death differently.
b: Greek hyper pantos can be 'for everyone' (masculine) or 'for everything' (neuter); the Plain, like the KJV ('for every man'), takes it as 'everyone'. The Catholic Catechism teaches that 'Christ died for all men without exception' (605). The Methodist Articles of Religion (20) call Christ's offering 'perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction for all the sins of the whole world'. The Canons of Dort (second main point) agree that Christ's death is 'more than sufficient to atone for the sins of the whole world' (article 3), but teach that God intended it to save effectively 'all those and only those who were chosen' (article 8); readers who hold this read 'everyone' here as each of the 'many sons' brought to glory (2:10) and the 'children' given to him (2:13). See the topic on the atonement.

p: Archēgos is the leader who goes first and opens the way, as in Acts 3:15 'the Founder of life'.
b: Archēgos joins archē, 'beginning, first place', with agō, 'lead'. It can mean a founder (of a city or a family), a leader who goes ahead of his people, a champion who fights for them, or the source of something. The site uses 'Founder' for Jesus in every place: "You put to death the Founder of life" (Acts 3:15); "as Founder and Savior" (Acts 5:31). Here the picture is a leader bringing a whole people into glory, walking the road ahead of them. Hebrews 12:2 calls him 'the Founder and perfecter of faith'.
orig: τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς σωτηρίας αὐτῶν (ton archēgon tēs sōtērias autōn)

t: Made perfect: brought to the goal
p: Teleioō does not mean Jesus was flawed; it means completed, made fit for the goal.
b: Teleioō comes from telos, 'end, goal'. To make something 'perfect' in this sense is to bring it to completion. The Son was never morally imperfect (4:15; 7:26). He was 'made perfect' by going through suffering, death and exaltation, so that he became fully qualified as Savior and high priest (5:9; 7:28). The word also had a priestly sense: in the Greek Old Testament, ordaining a priest is 'perfecting his hands' (Exodus 29:9; Leviticus 8:33). Hebrews uses the word family often, of Christ and of believers (10:14; 11:40; 12:23).

p: From one Father, from Adam, or from Abraham: the Greek just says 'from one'.
b: Greek ex henos leaves the noun out. (1) Most read 'from one Father', God, so that the Son and the 'many sons' share one Father. (2) Some read 'from one ancestor', Adam, stressing shared humanity (2:14). (3) Some read Abraham, since 2:16 speaks of 'Abraham's offspring'. All three make the same point: the one who makes holy and those made holy belong to one family, which is why he calls them brothers.

p: Greek adelphoi, plural, normally includes women. The site keeps 'brothers' with a gloss.
b: The plural adelphoi was the normal word for a group of brothers and sisters, as a family or a church. The site writes 'brothers' in the Plain (as in Acts and Romans), with the gloss 'brothers and sisters', so that the family image stays and readers know women are included. In 2:11-17 the point is that the Son is not ashamed to call human beings his siblings: he took on 'blood and flesh' (2:14) and became 'like his brothers in everything' (2:17).

a: I will spread the news of your name to my brothers
t: Psalm 22 on the lips of Jesus
p: The psalm that begins 'My God, my God' turns to praise in its second half. Hebrews puts that praise in Jesus' mouth.
b: The site's Psalm reads: "I will spread the news of your name to my brothers; / where the people gather, I will sing your praise." (Psalm 22:22). Psalm 22 opens with the cry Jesus spoke on the cross (Mark 15:34) and turns at verse 22 to thanks for rescue. Hebrews has the risen Son speak that verse: the one who suffered now praises God among his brothers. The Greek for 'assembly' is ekklēsia, the word the New Testament uses for the church: the risen Christ sings in the midst of his gathered people.

a: I will keep my trust in him
t: Isaiah's words in the Son's mouth
p: From the Greek of Isaiah 8:17. The Son, like Isaiah, trusts God while waiting.
b: The words match the Greek of Isaiah 8:17, pepoithōs esomai ep' autō; similar lines are in 2 Samuel 22:3 and Isaiah 12:2. The site's Isaiah, from the Hebrew, reads: "So I will wait on the LORD" and "I will keep looking to him." (Isaiah 8:17). Isaiah spoke when Judah's king refused to trust God, and he and his children stood as 'signs' (8:18). By putting these words in the Son's mouth, Hebrews shows Jesus as the faithful human being who lived by trust in God, the very thing the readers are called to do.

a: Look: I and the children God gave me
p: In Isaiah 8:18 the prophet's sons are living signs. Hebrews applies the line to Christ and his people.
b: The site's Isaiah reads: "Look at me and the children the LORD has given me: / we are signs and omens in Israel" (Isaiah 8:18). Isaiah's sons had names that preached (7:3; 8:3). Hebrews reads the line as the Son presenting his followers to God as his children, a family given to him by the Father. Compare John 17:6: 'the people you gave me'. The 'children' lead straight into 2:14: because the children have blood and flesh, so did he.

p: Hebrews says the Son 'took a share' in blood and flesh: a real human body, not a disguise.
b: The critical text has 'blood and flesh', an unusual order; the Byzantine text and the KJV have the more common 'flesh and blood'. Either way the phrase means human nature in its weakness and mortality (Matthew 16:17; 1 Corinthians 15:50). The verbs differ: the children 'have in common' (kekoinōnēken, perfect: it is their state), the Son 'took a share' (meteschen, aorist: a choice at a point in time). This is one of the plainest New Testament statements that the Son became fully human, so that he could die.
orig: κεκοινώνηκεν αἵματος καὶ σαρκός (kekoinōnēken haimatos kai sarkos)

a: the one who wields the might of death
p: How does the devil hold the power of death? And how did Jesus' death break it?
b: Hebrews does not explain, but its readers knew Jewish tradition that tied death to the devil from Eden on (Genesis 3; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24). Readings: (1) the devil accuses sinners, and death is the penalty sin earns; when Christ's death deals with sin, the accuser has nothing left (Colossians 2:14-15; Revelation 12:10). (2) The devil holds people by fear of death (2:15), and Christ, by dying and rising, shows death is not the end. (3) The early church's 'Christ the victor' picture: Christ entered death's realm and broke it from inside. The verb katargeō means to make ineffective, put out of action, not to annihilate.
r: Genesis 3:1-19; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24; Colossians 2:15; 1 John 3:8; Revelation 12:10; 1 Corinthians 15:54-57

t: Slavery to the fear of death
p: Fear of death was a theme across the ancient world; Hebrews calls it slavery.
b: Greek and Roman writers argued about how to face death without fear, and Jewish writings spoke of death as an enemy. Hebrews says that fear of death kept people slaves their whole lives: it made them cling to life, give in to pressure and protect themselves. The readers had faced loss and danger for their faith (10:32-34) and would face more (12:4). Freed from the fear of death, they could endure.

p: The KJV adds words in italics to make it about the incarnation. The Greek verb means to take hold of, to help.
b: Epilambanomai means to grasp, take hold of, often to help someone. The KJV reads 'he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham', with 'the nature of' in italics, showing words the translators supplied, so that the verse speaks of the incarnation. Most modern scholars read it as rescue: he does not reach out to help angels; he takes hold of Abraham's children. The Greek of Isaiah 41:9 uses a related verb of God taking hold of Israel, his servant, 'from the ends of the earth', and Hebrews 8:9 uses this one of God taking his people by the hand out of Egypt.

p: A Jewish way of naming God's people. Hebrews does not explain whether Gentiles are included.
b: 'The seed of Abraham' is the people of the promise (Genesis 22:17-18; Isaiah 41:8). Hebrews uses the phrase without the explanation Paul gives in Galatians, where all who belong to Christ are counted in: "Now if you belong to Christ, you are Abraham's offspring" (Galatians 3:29). Some read Hebrews' wording as a sign that its readers were largely Jewish believers; others note that the letter never discusses Jews and Gentiles at all and simply speaks of 'God's people' (4:9). See the audience on the book page.

t: The first time Jesus is called high priest
p: No other New Testament book calls Jesus a priest by title. Hebrews does so here for the first time.
b: The high priest of Israel was Aaron and his heirs: he alone entered the most holy place, once a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). No other New Testament book calls Jesus 'priest' or 'high priest' by title; F. F. Bruce (1964) called Hebrews 'the only New Testament document which expressly calls Him a priest, although His priesthood is implied in others', as John Baigent quotes him (1981). Hebrews names its theme here with two words, 'merciful' and 'faithful', and then expounds them in reverse order: faithful in 3:1-4:13, merciful in 4:14-5:10. Chapters 7-10 explain his priesthood in full.

a: to make atonement for the people's sins
p: Hilaskomai: to deal with sin so that the relationship with God is set right. Propitiate or expiate?
b: The verb hilaskomai in the Greek Old Testament renders Hebrew kipper, 'make atonement'. Readers debate whether it means to turn away God's anger (propitiation), to wipe out the sin (expiation), or both. Here the object is 'the sins' (not God), which leans toward wiping them out; but the setting is a priest acting 'in what concerns God', which keeps the relation to God in view. The same verb is in the tax collector's prayer: "God, be gracious to me, the sinner." (Luke 18:13). The related noun is the ark's lid in 9:5.
orig: εἰς τὸ ἱλάσκεσθαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας (eis to hilaskesthai tas hamartias)

p: Peirazō means both test and tempt. Jesus was tested by suffering, and that is how he can help.
b: English must choose between 'tempted' (enticed to sin) and 'tested' (put under pressure to see what holds). The Greek peirazō covers both. In Hebrews the setting is suffering: 'he has suffered through being tested'. The readers were being pressed by loss and shame to give up (10:32-39), and Jesus knew that pressure, in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11) and above all in Gethsemane and on the cross (5:7-8). 4:15 adds that he was tested in every way, but apart from sin.

p: The only place in the New Testament where Jesus is called 'apostle': the one sent from God.
b: Apostolos means 'one who is sent', an envoy. Nowhere else is Jesus given this title, though John's Gospel often says the Father 'sent' him (John 17:3, 18). The pair 'apostle and high priest' recalls Moses and Aaron: Moses was sent to speak for God to the people (Exodus 3:10), Aaron stood before God for the people. Jesus is both. Chapter 3 compares him with Moses; chapters 5-7 with Aaron.
orig: τὸν ἀπόστολον καὶ ἀρχιερέα (ton apostolon kai archierea)

p: Homologia: what believers say together about Jesus, perhaps a fixed creed used in worship.
b: Homologia means agreeing, saying the same thing, and so a public confession. Hebrews uses it three times, each time urging the readers to hold on to it: 3:1; 4:14 ('let us keep a strong hold on our confession'); 10:23 ('the confession of our hope'). It may have been a short creed spoken at baptism or in worship, such as 'Jesus is the Son of God' (4:14). The readers' danger was to go quiet about it under pressure.

p: The verb is 'made', but in Greek it can mean 'appointed' to an office, as with Moses and Aaron.
b: Most English versions translate tō poiēsanti auton as 'the one who appointed him', and that is the sense: God made him apostle and high priest. The Greek of 1 Samuel 12:6 uses the same verb: 'the Lord, who made Moses and Aaron', meaning who appointed them. The Plain keeps the literal 'made' so the reader sees the word. It does not say the Son was created; 1:2-3 has already said the ages were made through him.

a: as Moses also was in his house
p: Numbers 12:7: God defends Moses against Miriam and Aaron by calling him faithful in all his house.
b: When Miriam and Aaron criticized Moses, God answered: "Not so my servant Moses. / In all my house he is faithful." (Numbers 12:7). God spoke with Moses 'mouth to mouth', not in riddles. For Jewish readers there was no greater human figure. Hebrews does not run Moses down: it calls him faithful, quoting God's own praise, and then says the Son is greater, as the builder is greater than the house and a son is greater than a household servant (3:3-6).

p: Therapōn, from the Greek of Numbers 12:7: a trusted servant, not a slave, but still not the son.
b: Hebrews takes the word straight from the Greek of Numbers 12:7, ho therapōn mou Mōusēs. A therapōn was a personal attendant, a trusted aide; it is a word of honor, not the ordinary word for a slave (doulos). The contrast is between 'in' and 'over': Moses was faithful in the house as an attendant, Christ is faithful over the house as a Son (3:6). Moses' work was 'a witness to things that would be spoken later', so the law itself points ahead.

t: The house that is a people
p: In the Bible 'house' can mean a building, a household or a dynasty. Here God's house is his people.
b: In 2 Samuel 7 the word plays: David wants to build God a house (a temple), and God promises to build David a house (a dynasty). Numbers 12:7 speaks of Moses in God's 'house', meaning his household, Israel. Hebrews says believers are that house now, as 1 Peter 2:5 calls them living stones built into a spiritual house. The early manuscripts differ slightly ('which house we are' or 'whose house we are'), but the meaning is the same.

t: Boldness: the free speech of a citizen
p: Parrēsia was the free speech of citizens. In Hebrews it is the confidence to come before God.
b: Parrēsia in Greek cities was a citizen's right to speak freely in the assembly. Acts uses it for the apostles speaking out without fear ('freedom of speech', the site's term there). In Hebrews it turns toward God: believers have 'boldness' to come near the throne of grace (4:16) and to enter the sanctuary (10:19), and they must not throw it away (10:35). Here it is something to 'hold on to': a public, unashamed confidence in front of a hostile world.

p: Hebrews introduces Psalm 95 as the Holy Spirit speaking in the present tense: 'says'.
b: The verb is present: the Spirit 'says', not 'said'. For Hebrews, Scripture is God's living voice speaking to the readers now, which is the whole point of the psalm's 'Today'. The same formula comes back at 10:15 for Jeremiah 31. In 4:7 the writer adds that God spoke these words 'in David', but the human author matters less than the speaker, as with 'someone, somewhere' in 2:6.

a: Today, if you hear his voice
t: Psalm 95: a call to worship and a warning
p: Psalm 95 begins 'Come, let us sing' and ends with God's warning about the wilderness.
b: The site's Psalm reads: "Today, if you would only listen to his voice!" (Psalm 95:7), and then: "Do not make your hearts hard, as at Meribah" (Psalm 95:8). Hebrews quotes the Greek of Psalm 95:7-11 (94:7-11 in the Greek numbering), then explains it phrase by phrase down to 4:11, a kind of sermon on a text. The readers are like Israel between Egypt and Canaan: rescued, not yet arrived, and tempted to turn back.

p: The Hebrew has the place names Meribah and Massah. The Greek translated the names into ordinary words.
b: In Hebrew, Psalm 95:8 names two places: Meribah ('quarrel') and Massah ('testing'), where Israel complained for water (Exodus 17:7; Numbers 20:13). The site's Exodus explains: "He called the place Massah and Meribah, because the Israelites picked a fight there" (Exodus 17:7). The Greek translators turned the names into nouns: parapikrasmos, 'embitterment, bitter provocation', and peirasmos, 'testing'. Hebrews quotes the Greek. The Plain uses capitals, 'the Bitter Quarrel' and 'the Testing', so that readers can see they began as names.

p: In the psalm God was disgusted for forty years. Hebrews joins the forty years to Israel seeing God's works.
b: The Greek psalm (94:9-10) runs: 'they saw my works. For forty years I felt disgust at that generation.' Hebrews adds the word 'So' (dio) after 'forty years', which makes the forty years belong to Israel watching God's works: forty years of miracles, and still they did not trust. In 3:17 Hebrews returns to the psalm's own link ('Whom did he feel disgust at for forty years?'). Both are true in Numbers. The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'tested me, proved me' where the critical text has 'tested by testing'; the meaning hardly changes.
orig: καὶ εἶδον τὰ ἔργα μου τεσσεράκοντα ἔτη· διὸ

t: Claude's theory: a second forty years
p: Did the writer think of forty years from Jesus' ministry to his readers' own day?
b: Claude's theory, offered as a possibility. By moving 'forty years' so that it covers Israel watching God's works (see the note on 3:9), Hebrews may be inviting the readers to count their own years. If Hebrews was written in the 60s AD, about a generation had passed since Jesus' ministry and the 'signs and wonders' of 2:4, and the Temple was still standing (as 8:4, 13 and 10:1-2 may suggest). The warning would then be pointed: Israel had forty years of wonders and fell in the wilderness; do not do the same in your forty years. This rests on 3:9-10, 3:17 and 2:3-4, and on the date being before AD 70. A Jewish reading of the same verse also counts the psalm's forty years forward: in the Talmud Rabbi Eliezer says 'The messianic era will be forty years long', citing Psalm 95:10 (Bavli Sanhedrin 99a). That is not the same idea, but it shows that the psalm's forty years could be read as more than the wilderness.

a: They will never come into my rest
t: An oath with a missing half
p: Greek 'if they enter my rest' copies a Hebrew oath form meaning 'they will never enter'.
b: The Greek reads literally 'if they will enter my rest', copying a Hebrew way of swearing: 'May such-and-such happen to me if they enter!' with the curse left unsaid. It means a firm 'never'. 'My rest' in the psalm was the land of Canaan, where Israel would settle in peace (Deuteronomy 12:9), and also God's own resting place, the temple on Zion: "This is my place of rest forever and ever." (Psalm 132:14). Hebrews will add a third: God's own Sabbath rest since creation (4:4).
orig: εἰ εἰσελεύσονται εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν μου

p: Apostēnai, 'stand away from', gives the English word apostasy.
b: The verb aphistēmi means to stand off from, desert, rebel. Its noun is the source of 'apostasy'. The danger in Hebrews is not that the readers might pick a different god, but that they might walk away from 'the living God', perhaps back to a safer life inside the synagogue or away from the faith altogether. 'Living God' is an Old Testament title (Deuteronomy 5:26; Joshua 3:10) that Hebrews uses four times (3:12; 9:14; 10:31; 12:22).
orig: ἐν τῷ ἀποστῆναι ἀπὸ θεοῦ ζῶντος

a: keep urging each other on day by day
t: A church that met and talked
p: The cure for a hard heart is other believers, every day. Hebrews assumes a close community.
b: The verb parakaleō means to urge, encourage, comfort or warn. The writer calls his own work 'this word of exhortation' (13:22), from the same root. He does not expect the readers to stay faithful alone: they are to speak to each other daily, as long as 'Today' lasts. Some of them had begun to skip their gatherings (10:25). A believer cut off from the others is the one most easily tricked by sin.

p: Metochoi again: sharers with Christ, or companions of the Messiah, like the king's partners in 1:9.
b: Metochoi tou Christou can mean 'sharers in Christ' (in union with him) or 'companions of the Christ', the anointed king, recalling 'above your partners' in 1:9, where the anointed king has companions. The Greek has the article ('the Christ'), which fits the second sense: believers are the Messiah's companions, sharing his kingdom. Either way the condition follows: 'as long as we keep... steady until the end'.

p: The word at 1:3 for God's 'being' here means confidence, firm footing.
b: Tēn archēn tēs hypostaseōs is 'the beginning of the hypostasis'. At 1:3 the word meant God's very being; at 11:1 it will mean the 'assurance' of what is hoped for. Here it means firm confidence, a footing that holds. Some read 'the beginning of our confidence' as the first trust the readers had at their conversion (compare 10:32, 'the days before'). The Plain gives a different English word in each place and notes the link.
orig: τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς ὑποστάσεως (tēn archēn tēs hypostaseōs)

a: whose corpses dropped in the wilderness
p: From Numbers 14, after the spies' report: the generation that refused to go in would die outside.
b: God's sentence on the generation that refused to enter Canaan was: "In this wilderness your dead bodies will fall" (Numbers 14:29). The Greek kōla is 'limbs, carcasses', the word the Greek of Numbers uses there. Paul draws the same lesson in 1 Corinthians 10:5-11: these things happened as warnings for us. The readers had come out of their 'Egypt' and were in danger of dying short of the land.
orig: ὧν τὰ κῶλα ἔπεσεν (hōn ta kōla epesen)

p: Hebrews treats 'refused to obey' (3:18) and 'unbelief' (3:19) as two names for one failure.
b: 3:18 says those who 'refused to obey' (apeithēsasin) did not enter; 3:19 says it was 'unbelief' (apistian). In Greek the two words differ by a single letter-sound, and in Hebrews they are two sides of one thing: not trusting God is shown in not obeying him, and not obeying comes from not trusting. Numbers 14:11 has God ask: how long will they not believe in me? Faith in Hebrews is never only an opinion; it acts (chapter 11).

t: A fear that keeps you safe
p: Hebrews urges fear, the kind that keeps a traveler on the road, not terror before a cruel God.
b: Phobēthōmen is 'let us fear'. Hebrews holds together boldness before God's throne (4:16) and fear of falling short (4:1; 10:31; 12:28-29). The fear is not of God's character but of missing what God offers: the promise 'is still left open', and one could be 'judged to have missed it'. The verb hysterēkenai, 'to have come too late, fallen behind', is used again of missing God's grace in 12:15.

a: had the good news announced to us
p: The verb is euangelizō, 'tell good news': Israel in the wilderness had a gospel, the promise of rest.
b: Hebrews uses the verb from which 'gospel' comes for both groups: 'we, like them, have had the good news announced'. For Israel the good news was the promise of the land and rest; for the readers it is the message about Christ. The comparison is exact: the same God, the same kind of promise, the same danger of not trusting it. Paul makes a similar comparison in 1 Corinthians 10:1-4, where Israel too had food and drink from Christ.

a: We who have come to believe are going into rest
p: The verb is present tense. Is the rest entered now, at death, or at the end?
b: Greek eiserchometha is present: 'we are entering'. (1) Some read a present rest: believers already enter God's rest by faith, a peace of conscience and of trust (compare Matthew 11:28-29). (2) Most read the present as sure future: 'we are on our way in', since 4:1 and 4:11 still urge the readers to strive to enter. (3) Some think of the heavenly homeland and city of 11:10-16 and 12:22, entered fully at the end. Hebrews' 'already and not yet' (2:8-9) allows a little of each: the rest is open now and completed later.

a: And on the seventh day God rested from all his works
p: Genesis 2:2: God's own rest began on the seventh day and has no recorded end.
b: The site's Genesis reads: "and on the seventh day he rested from all the work he had been doing." (Genesis 2:2). Hebrews links Psalm 95's 'my rest' to God's own Sabbath rest after creation by a Jewish method of reading in which one word ties two passages together (the Greek of both uses words built on katapau-, 'rest'). Each of the first six days in Genesis ends with 'Evening came, and morning came', for example "Evening came, and morning came: the sixth day." (Genesis 1:31). The seventh day has no such ending. Hebrews' argument fits that silence: God's rest is still going on, and his people are invited into it.

p: The Hebrew Psalm 95 has no title. The Greek gives it one: 'A praise of song, of David'.
b: In the Hebrew Bible Psalm 95 has no heading. The Greek Psalter (94:1) begins with the title Ainos ōdēs tō Dauid, 'A praise of song, of David', and Hebrews, reading the Greek, says God spoke 'in David'. 'In David' may also mean simply 'in the book of David', that is, the Psalms. The argument is about time: David lived centuries after Joshua brought Israel into Canaan, and still God said 'Today'. So the land was not the final rest.

p: The Greek name is Iēsous, the same as Jesus. The KJV reads 'Jesus' here, which confuses many readers.
b: Joshua's Hebrew name Yehoshua became Iēsous in Greek, the same form as Jesus' name. The KJV printed 'Jesus' here (and in Acts 7:45), and readers have wondered how Jesus gave Israel rest. It means Joshua son of Nun, who led Israel into Canaan. Hebrews may enjoy the double meaning: the first Iēsous gave only a partial rest; the second leads into the real one.

p: Hebrews switches from 'rest' to sabbatismos, 'Sabbath-keeping': rest as celebration, not only stopping.
b: Until now the word has been katapausis, 'rest'. Here Hebrews uses sabbatismos, 'a Sabbath-keeping, a Sabbath rest'. It is found nowhere else in the Bible; Thayer's lexicon lists one other early use, in Plutarch's essay On Superstition (chapter 3). It comes from the verb in Exodus 16:30 Greek, 'the people kept Sabbath'. The word suggests the joy and worship of the seventh day, not only an end to work. 'God's people' still have it waiting for them.

a: The one who has gone into his rest
t: Who is 'the one who has gone in'?
p: Usually any believer who enters God's rest. A minority think of Jesus himself.
b: (1) Most read the verse as a general statement: whoever enters God's rest stops their own labor, as God did on the seventh day. Some take the 'works' as the hard labor of this life (Revelation 14:13, 'they will rest from their labors'), others as trying to earn God's favor. (2) A minority read 'the one who has gone in' as Jesus, the forerunner who has entered (6:20) and rests from his works as God did from his; then 4:11 urges the readers to follow him in. Both readings fit Hebrews' picture of a pilgrim people following their leader.

a: The word of God is alive and at work
p: Not first the Bible as a book, but God speaking, as he has just spoken in Psalm 95.
b: In context 'the word of God' is what God says, as in Psalm 95 ('Today, if you hear his voice'). It is 'alive' (zōn) and 'at work' (energēs, the root of 'energy'). Christians apply the verse to Scripture, which is where they hear God speak; it is not here a title of Christ, as 'the Word' is in John 1:1. The Plain keeps lowercase 'word', as Hebrews uses it of God's speech (also 6:5; 11:3; 13:7).
orig: ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ (ho logos tou theou)

p: The Greek says 'two-mouthed': a blade sharpened on both sides that 'eats' both ways.
b: Distomos, 'two-mouthed', is a blade with two cutting edges; machaira was the short sword or long knife, also used for sacrifice and surgery. The same picture appears in Revelation: "a sharp two-edged sword was coming out of his mouth" (Revelation 1:16), and in Isaiah 49:2 ('he made my mouth like a sharp sword'). The Wisdom of Solomon pictures God's all-powerful word leaping from heaven like a warrior with a sharp sword (Wisdom of Solomon 18:15-16).
r: Revelation 1:16; Revelation 19:15; Isaiah 49:2; Ephesians 6:17; Wisdom of Solomon 18:15-16

a: where soul and spirit are divided
t: Soul and spirit: two parts or one?
p: Some read here a human being in three parts (body, soul, spirit). Most read a picture of the word reaching the depths.
b: (1) Some Christians, called trichotomists, see body, soul and spirit as three distinct parts of a person and point to this verse with 1 Thessalonians 5:23. (2) Most commentators read a picture, not a lesson in anatomy: the word cuts deeper than any blade, to the place where you could no longer tell soul from spirit, or joint from marrow. The second half says the same thing plainly: it judges the 'musings and plans of the heart'. Nothing in a person is hidden from it (4:13).

p: Trachēlizō comes from the word for 'neck': a wrestler's hold, or a sacrifice with its neck bent back.
b: The verb trachēlizō is built on trachēlos, 'neck'. Thayer's lexicon gives two uses: of fighters who 'seize and twist the neck or throat' of an opponent, and of bending back 'the neck of the victim to be slain', so that the throat lies bare; from that, 'to lay bare, expose'. Either picture is vivid: before God every creature is pinned, exposed, unable to hide its face. The Plain says 'laid wide open'.

a: the one we will have to answer to
p: The Greek ends 'to whom our logos': the same word as 'the word of God' in 4:12, here meaning 'account'.
b: The last words are pros hon hēmin ho logos, literally 'to whom (is) our word'. Logos can mean 'word', 'reason' or 'account', as in giving account. So the paragraph begins with God's logos addressing us (4:12) and ends with our logos, the account we must give him (4:13). The Plain cannot keep the pun, so it gives the sense: the one we will have to answer to. 13:17 uses the same phrase of leaders who must 'give an account'.

p: Once a year the high priest passed through the tent into the most holy place. Jesus passed through the heavens.
b: Once a year the high priest went through the outer room of the tent and behind the veil into the most holy place (Leviticus 16:2, 12). Hebrews pictures heaven as a greater sanctuary (8:1-5; 9:11, 24), and Jesus has gone through its outer layers to God's very presence. 'The heavens' is plural, as often in Jewish thought, where the heavens were several layers; Paul speaks of 'the third heaven' (2 Corinthians 12:2). This verse picks up the theme of 2:17 and begins the central section of the book.

a: feel for us in our weaknesses
p: Sympatheō is 'suffer with'. The high priest does not look down on weakness; he has felt it.
b: Sympathēsai is the root of 'sympathy', 'to suffer with'. It is more than pity: it is shared feeling from the inside. Hebrews 10:34 uses the same verb of the readers who 'felt for the prisoners'. 'Weaknesses' (astheneiai) are not sins but the frailty that makes sin and fear easy: tiredness, pain, fear of death (2:15; 5:2, 7).

t: Tested in every way, but without sin
p: All Christian traditions confess that Jesus did not sin. They have argued over whether he could have.
b: The New Testament says it in many places: "God made the one who did not know sin to be sin for us" (2 Corinthians 5:21); see also 1 Peter 2:22 and 1 John 3:5. Two questions follow. (1) Was the testing real if he could not fall? Some theologians say he was 'able not to sin' and truly could have; others say he was 'not able to sin', because he is God the Son, and answer that the testing was still real, since only one who does not give in feels the full force of temptation. (2) Does 'apart from sin' mean he was tested in every way except by sinful desires from within? Many read it that way. Either way, Hebrews' point is that he can help us (2:18; 4:16).

p: Proserchomai was the word for a priest approaching the altar. In Hebrews every believer comes near.
b: In the Greek Old Testament the verb is used of priests approaching God's altar: Moses tells Aaron, 'Come near to the altar' (Leviticus 9:7, Proselthe). Ordinary Israelites could not come near the most holy place. Hebrews uses the verb seven times (4:16; 7:25; 10:1, 22; 11:6; 12:18, 22), always of coming to God, and now it is for all believers. The Plain renders it 'come near' each time.

p: God's throne, which might have meant judgment, becomes the place where mercy is handed out.
b: In the tent, God was pictured as enthroned above the cherubim on the ark's lid, the atonement lid (Exodus 25:22; 1 Samuel 4:4), the place where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14-15). Hebrews calls God's throne 'the throne of grace': because our high priest is there, it is a place to receive mercy, 'at just the right time' (eukairon, timely help, as when one is in trouble).

p: Hebrews gives two marks of a true high priest: he is one of the people, and God calls him.
b: The law chose Aaron 'from among the Israelites': "bring your brother Aaron near you, with his sons, out from among the Israelites, to be my priests" (Exodus 28:1). Hebrews draws two marks from the law: a high priest shares the weakness of those he serves (5:1-3), and he does not appoint himself (5:4). Then it shows that Christ has both (5:5-10), in reverse order. In the century before the readers, Herod the Great removed and appointed high priests at will, and the Roman governor Valerius Gratus replaced four in a few years (Josephus, Antiquities 15.3.1; 18.2.2), a contrast the first readers may have felt.

p: Two words for offerings: gifts (dōra) and sacrifices (thysiai). Hebrews uses the pair again in 8:3 and 9:9.
b: Dōra are gifts; thysiai are sacrifices, usually of animals. Together they cover the whole range of offerings in Leviticus 1-7, from grain offerings to sin offerings. Hebrews uses the pair three times (5:1; 8:3; 9:9), always of what the priests of the tent offered, to set up the contrast with the one offering Christ made of himself (7:27; 10:10-14).
orig: δῶρά τε καὶ θυσίας (dōra te kai thysias)

p: Metriopatheō: to keep one's feelings in measure, neither harsh nor careless.
b: The verb joins metrios, 'measured, moderate', and pathos, 'feeling'. A good priest is neither furious with sinners nor indifferent to sin: he deals with them gently because he knows his own weakness. It is a different verb from 'feel for us' in 4:15 (sympatheō): the human priest is kept from harshness by his own frailty; Christ, who never sinned, goes further and suffers with us.

a: people who do wrong without knowing or who wander off course
p: The law offered sacrifices for sins done in ignorance or by straying, not for sin done 'with a high hand'.
b: Leviticus 4 provides sin offerings when someone sins 'by mistake' (4:2, 13, 22, 27). Numbers 15:27-31 sets that against sin done defiantly, 'with a high hand', for which no offering is given and the person is cut off. Hebrews keeps the distinction: the high priest deals gently with the ignorant and the straying, and later Hebrews warns that for those who 'keep on sinning by choice' 'there is no longer any sacrifice for sins left' (10:26). On the Day of Atonement the high priest offered for 'the sins the people committed in ignorance' (9:7).

t: A priest who needs atonement himself
p: On the Day of Atonement Aaron first offered a bull for himself and his house.
b: Leviticus 16:6 and 16:11 have the high priest offer a bull for his own sin and his household's before he offers for the people. In the Greek of Leviticus 9:7 Moses tells Aaron to make atonement 'for yourself and for your house' and then 'for them'. Hebrews will make a point of the contrast in 7:27: Christ had no need to offer for himself.

p: Aaron did not take the priesthood; God gave it. Korah's revolt showed what happens to those who grab it.
b: God chose Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1). When Korah and his followers claimed the right to serve as priests, the ground swallowed them (Numbers 16), and Aaron's staff budded to show God's choice (Numbers 17). Hebrews will mention that staff at 9:4. King Uzziah was struck with skin disease for burning incense, a priest's task (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). Honor in the priesthood comes from being called.

a: did not give himself the glory
p: Like John's Gospel: the Son receives his honor from the Father.
b: John's Jesus says the same: "If I give myself glory, my glory is worth nothing. The one who gives me glory is my Father" (John 8:54). Hebrews joins the two verses of the two royal psalms: Psalm 2:7 ('You are my son') and Psalm 110:4 ('You are a priest forever'). The one who called him Son also made him priest. That joining is the heart of Hebrews' teaching: the Son is the priest.

p: Greek taxis is 'order, rank'. The site's Psalm 110:4 renders the Hebrew 'after the pattern'.
b: The Greek kata tēn taxin Melchisedek means 'according to the order (rank, arrangement) of Melchizedek', and 'order' is the usual English. The site's Psalm 110:4, from the Hebrew 'al-dibrati, reads 'after the pattern of Melchizedek', and the Plain of Hebrews keeps that wording every time the line comes back (5:6, 10; 6:20; 7:11, 17), so the reader can follow the quotation. The phrase does not mean that there was a line of Melchizedek priests: there is only one, and Christ is like him. In 7:15 Hebrews explains it as 'in the likeness of Melchizedek'.
orig: κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισέδεκ (kata tēn taxin Melchisedek)

p: The psalm's oath that the king is also a priest: the verse behind chapters 5-7.
b: The site's Psalm reads: "You are a priest forever, / after the pattern of Melchizedek." (Psalm 110:4). Psalm 110 is addressed to a king of David's line in Jerusalem, the city once ruled by Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem (Genesis 14:18). Israel's kings were from Judah and could not be Levitical priests, so a royal priesthood had to be 'after another pattern'. Hebrews quotes or alludes to the line at 5:6, 10; 6:20; 7:3, 11, 15, 17, 21, 24 and 28.

a: While he lived in the flesh
p: Requests, loud cries and tears to the one who could save him from death: most readers think of Gethsemane.
b: The Gospels tell how Jesus prayed in the garden: "Abba, Father," he was saying, "for you anything is possible. Make this cup pass me by." (Mark 14:36). Luke adds that "His sweat came like clots of blood dripping onto the ground." (Luke 22:44). None of the Gospels mentions tears in Gethsemane, so some readers think Hebrews also has the cross in view (Mark 15:34, 37), or that the words reflect the psalms of the suffering righteous, such as Psalm 22:24: "when the man called to him for help, he listened." (Psalm 22:24). 'In the flesh' means his earthly, mortal life. The verb for 'offered up' (prosenenkas) is the one Hebrews uses for a priest offering gifts and sacrifices (5:1, 3): his prayers were a priest's offering.

a: because of his reverence he was heard
p: If he was heard, why did he die? Readers answer in different ways; one proposal changes the text.
b: Eisakoustheis apo tēs eulabeias: 'heard from (because of) his reverence'. (1) Most read 'heard because of his reverence': God answered his prayer not by sparing him death but by raising him out of it (note the Greek 'out of death', ek thanatou). (2) The KJV takes apo as 'from' and eulabeia as fear: 'was heard in that he feared', that is, rescued from his fear and strengthened to go on. (3) Some have supposed the text is corrupt and added 'not' (ouk): 'he was not heard'. James Swetnam (2000), surveying the proposals, answers that 'no manuscript has the' 'not'. Swetnam himself sets the plea at the cross, where Jesus prayed Psalm 22, and argues that eulabeia in Hebrews means reverence, not terror (compare 12:28 and the related verb in 11:7).
r: Hebrews 12:28; Hebrews 11:7; Mark 14:36; Mark 15:34; Psalm 22:1; Acts 2:24

a: the things he suffered taught him obedience
p: The Greek rhymes: emathen aph' hōn epathen, 'he learned from what he suffered'.
b: Emathen aph' hōn epathen is a play on a Greek saying that people learn by suffering (mathein, 'learn'; pathein, 'suffer'). Hebrews uses it of the Son, which is startling: he was not disobedient before, but he learned what obedience costs by doing it all the way to death (Philippians 2:8). The Plain cannot keep the rhyme. 'Even though he was a Son' marks the surprise: sons in the ancient world were trained by discipline, as 12:5-11 says of believers, and this Son went through it too.
orig: ἔμαθεν ἀφ᾽ ὧν ἔπαθεν (emathen aph' hōn epathen)

p: Aitios: the cause or source. And the salvation is 'for everyone who obeys him'.
b: Aitios means the one responsible for something, its cause. Hebrews often adds 'eternal' to Christ's work: eternal salvation (5:9), eternal judgment (6:2), eternal redemption (9:12), eternal Spirit (9:14), eternal inheritance (9:15), eternal covenant (13:20). Note the link with 5:8: he learned obedience, and he saves those who obey him. Isaiah 45:17 speaks of Israel saved 'with an everlasting salvation'.

p: Nōthros, 'sluggish, lazy', frames this warning: here and in 6:12.
b: Nōthroi means slow, dull, lazy. It appears only twice in the New Testament, here ('your hearing has gone sluggish') and at 6:12 ('so you do not turn sluggish'), framing the section 5:11-6:12. The problem is not intelligence but willingness. The writer wants to go on to the deep teaching about Melchizedek (7:1-28), but first he stops to shake them awake.

a: the basic elements, the first lessons, of God's sayings
p: Stoicheia were the letters of the alphabet: they need to be taught their ABCs again.
b: Stoicheia were the basic elements of anything: the letters a child learns, or the elements of the world (the site's 'basic elements' in Galatians 4:3). Here it is the ABCs of the faith. Logia, 'sayings', are God's spoken words, 'oracles', the same word as Acts 7:38 ('living sayings') and Romans 3:2. The writer is gently sarcastic: by now they should be teachers.
orig: τὰ στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν λογίων τοῦ θεοῦ

p: Paul uses the same picture with the Corinthians, and Peter in a kinder sense.
b: Paul told the Corinthians: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, because you were not yet able." (1 Corinthians 3:2). 1 Peter 2:2 uses milk positively: crave the pure spiritual milk. Hebrews uses it as a rebuke, but with hope: in 6:1-3 it says, let us go on. The 'solid food' is the teaching about Christ as high priest after the pattern of Melchizedek in chapter 7.

p: Readings: teaching about being made right with God, moral teaching, or simply grown-up speech.
b: Logos dikaiosynēs, 'word of righteousness'. (1) Teaching about how God makes people right with himself, the heart of the gospel (compare Romans 1:17). (2) Moral instruction, the knowledge of right and wrong that 5:14 speaks of ('tell good and bad apart'). (3) Some take it in the plain sense of the picture: a baby cannot yet understand adult speech, 'right' or correct talk. The context of training and discerning (5:14) favors (2), with (1) in the background.

t: The mature: the same root as 'perfect'
p: Teleioi means grown-up, mature. Its root is the root of 'make perfect' (2:10) and 'full growth' (6:1).
b: Babies (nēpioi) and grown-ups (teleioi) are set side by side. Teleios is from telos, 'goal'; the same family gives 'make perfect' (2:10; 5:9; 7:28) and 'full growth' (teleiotēs, 6:1). The readers' maturity is meant to match what Christ has done: he was brought to the goal, and they are to be carried on toward it. Paul too uses teleioi for the mature (1 Corinthians 2:6; Philippians 3:15).

p: Gegymnasmena, 'trained', is the word that gives us 'gymnasium'.
b: The verb gymnazō was what athletes did in the gymnasion. Their 'senses' (aisthētēria, the faculties of perception) have been exercised by 'habit' (hexis, a settled condition built by practice). Hebrews returns to athletic training at 12:11, where discipline 'trains' those who go through it, using the same verb.

p: Literally 'the word of the beginning of Christ': basic teaching about Christ, or Christ's own first teaching.
b: Ton tēs archēs tou Christou logon can mean the basic teaching about Christ, or the elementary teaching that Christ himself began. 'Leave behind' does not mean abandon, but move on from, as a builder leaves the foundation to put up walls. 'Be carried on' is passive: growth is something God does, as 6:3 says, 'if God lets us'.
orig: τὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ λόγον

a: repentance from dead works and faith in God
t: A foundation any Jew could share
p: All six foundation stones in 6:1-2 were Jewish teaching too. What made them Christian was Christ.
b: Repentance, faith in God, washings, laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment all had roots in Jewish teaching and practice. Some readers see the point here: the readers could hold all these and still drift back into a Judaism without Jesus, which is why the writer will not lay this foundation again but go on to Christ the high priest. 'Dead works' are deeds that lead to death or have no life in them; 9:14 says Christ's blood cleans the conscience 'from dead works'. Some read them as sins, others as the rituals of the old order.

p: The Greek baptismōn is plural. The KJV has 'baptisms'; most think of purity washings and baptism together.
b: Baptismos (plural here) is used of Jewish washings of cups and pots (Mark 7:4) and of the tent's 'different kinds of washing' (Hebrews 9:10). It is not baptisma, the usual word for Christian baptism. So 'teaching about washings' likely meant explaining how Christian baptism differs from Jewish washings and John's baptism (Acts 19:1-5). The KJV's 'the doctrine of baptisms' points the same way.

p: Used in blessing, healing, giving the Spirit and setting people apart for service.
b: In Israel hands were laid on a sacrifice (Leviticus 1:4; 16:21), on Joshua to give him Moses' authority (Numbers 27:18-23), and in blessing (Genesis 48:14). In the early church hands were laid on the newly baptized to receive the Spirit ("So the two began to lay their hands on them, and the people received the Holy Spirit." Acts 8:17), on the sick (Mark 16:18) and on those set apart for service (Acts 6:6; 1 Timothy 4:14). Churches later linked the practice to confirmation and ordination.
r: Leviticus 1:4; Numbers 27:18-23; Acts 8:17; Acts 6:6; 1 Timothy 4:14; Acts 19:6

t: Enlightened: an early name for baptism
p: Phōtisthentas, 'enlightened'. By the 100s Christians called baptism 'illumination'.
b: The verb phōtizō means 'give light, enlighten'. Justin Martyr, writing about AD 155, explains baptism and says: 'this washing is called illumination, because they who learn these things are illuminated in their understandings' (First Apology 61). Many read Hebrews 6:4 as speaking of baptized believers. 'Once' (hapax) means once for all, an event that need not be repeated. Hebrews uses the same verb at 10:32 ('after you had received the light').

t: Tasted: a full meal or a sample?
p: Some read 'tasted' as real experience of salvation; others as a taste short of the real thing.
b: The verb 'taste' comes twice (6:4, 5). (1) Many read it as real experience, as when Jesus 'tasted death' (2:9), which was full. On this reading the people described are true believers. (2) Others, especially in the Reformed tradition, read 'tasted' as a sample that stops short of feeding: they experienced the gospel's power in the church without being born again. The 'gift from heaven' may be salvation, the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38), or, as some have read it, the Lord's Supper. The traditions card on this chapter sets out the churches' views.

p: Can a true believer fall away beyond return? The churches have answered in at least four ways.
b: (1) Real believers can fall away, and this describes it: Arminian and Wesleyan readers. John Wesley wrote on 6:6, 'Here is not a supposition, but a plain relation of fact'. (2) The people never had saving faith; they tasted but were not reborn. Calvin read the passage of 'a total defection or falling away from the Gospel', and held that 'some knowledge even in the reprobate' can afterwards vanish. (3) It is a real warning that God uses to keep his own from falling: Thomas Schreiner and Ardel Caneday (2001) call the warnings 'the means God uses to save and preserve his people to the end'. (4) Thomas Aquinas, with John Chrysostom and Ambrose before him, read it as ruling out a second baptism, not repentance: it is 'impossible to be renewed again, i.e., baptized'. See the card, which sets out what the churches teach.

a: impossible to make them new again and bring them to repentance
t: The early church and second repentance
p: Tertullian used this verse against forgiving serious sins after baptism. The Novatians did too.
b: Tertullian quoted Hebrews 6:4-6 (which he thought was by Barnabas) to argue that an adulterer could not be restored after baptism: the writer 'never knew of any second repentance promised by apostles to the adulterer and fornicator' (On Modesty 20). The Novatians, who refused to restore Christians who had fallen in persecution, appealed to the same passage. Ambrose answered them that it refers to the impossibility of being baptized again. Calvin later wrote that because 'the Novatians armed themselves with it', some in the Western church refused the letter's authority. Luther called it 'a hard knot'.

a: crucifying the Son of God over again
p: In ordinary Greek anastauroō simply means 'crucify'. Most take it here as 'crucify again'.
b: Thayer's lexicon says anastauroō means 'to raise up upon a cross, crucify', and is found very often in Greek writers from Herodotus on with that sense; it also notes that 'crucify again' has been defended for Hebrews 6:6, though Greek writers give no example of it. Most translations, ancient and modern, read 'again', because the people described once confessed Christ and now side with those who crucified him. The participles can also be read 'as long as they keep crucifying': on that reading the impossibility lasts only while they persist.
orig: ἀνασταυροῦντας ἑαυτοῖς τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ

a: ground that soaks up the rain
p: A picture from farming: the same rain falls on both fields; what grows shows what the field is.
b: The picture recalls Isaiah's song of the vineyard, which God tended and which produced only bad grapes (Isaiah 5:1-7), and Jesus' parable of the soils (Mark 4:3-20). Both fields have had the rain, as the people in 6:4-5 have had God's gifts. What they produce shows their condition. 'Thorns and thistles' echo the curse on the ground after Adam's sin: "Thorn and thistle it will sprout for you" (Genesis 3:18).

a: It ends up in the fire
p: Farmers burned off weeds to clear a field. Is the fire final judgment or a purging?
b: (1) Most read the fire as God's judgment, as in 10:27 ('the fury of a fire about to eat up those who stand against him') and 12:29 ('a devouring fire'). (2) Some note that a farmer burns a field to clear it of weeds, not to destroy the land, and read a purging that may lead to new growth. The writer says the land is 'close to' a curse, not yet under it, and turns at once to hope (6:9).

p: Right after the severest warning, the writer calls the readers 'beloved' for the only time.
b: Agapētoi is the word Jude uses ('Beloved', Jude 1:3) and the site renders it the same way. It comes only here in Hebrews, right after 6:4-8. The writer is not accusing his readers of having fallen away; he is warning them because he is sure of 'better things' in their case. The warning and the comfort belong together.

p: The readers had helped fellow believers in need, and still did.
b: 'The saints' (hagioi) are God's holy people, all believers (gloss at first use). Their service is described more fully in 10:32-34: they stood by those who were publicly insulted, visited prisoners and accepted the loss of their property. 13:1-3 asks them to keep it up. The verb is diakoneō, 'serve', from which 'deacon' comes. God will not forget such work, as Jesus said of a cup of cold water given to a disciple (Matthew 10:42).

a: he swore an oath by himself
p: After Abraham offered Isaac, God swore by himself to bless him.
b: The oath comes from the end of the binding of Isaac: "By myself I swear, says the LORD: because you have done this and have not held back your son, your only one," (Genesis 22:16). People swear by something greater than themselves; God has nothing greater, so he swears by himself. Hebrews will build its argument for hope on that oath (6:17-18), and an oath again sets up Christ's priesthood (7:20-22).

a: I will bless you richly, and I will multiply you greatly
p: Hebrews quotes the Greek of Genesis 22:17 but says 'multiply you' where Genesis has 'your offspring'.
b: The Greek doubles the verbs, 'blessing I will bless you and multiplying I will multiply you', a copy of a Hebrew way of stressing an action; the site's Genesis reads: "I will bless you richly and make your offspring as many as the stars in the sky" (Genesis 22:17). Hebrews shortens 'your offspring' to 'you', keeping the focus on Abraham himself, who had to wait (6:15). The Greek of Genesis begins ei mēn, 'surely', and the Byzantine text of Hebrews has the classical spelling ē mēn.
orig: εἰ μὴν εὐλογῶν εὐλογήσω σε (ei mēn eulogōn eulogēsō se)

a: stepped in between with an oath
p: Mesiteuō: to act as a go-between or guarantor. God stood surety for his own promise.
b: The verb mesiteuō comes from mesitēs, 'mediator', a word Hebrews uses of Christ as 'mediator' of a better covenant (8:6; 9:15; 12:24). Here God himself 'mediates' with an oath: he steps into the middle, putting himself up as the guarantee. 'Two unchangeable things' (6:18) are the promise and the oath. Since God cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2), either alone would be enough; both together are for our sake.

a: we who have run to him for safety
