p: Katapheugō is 'flee for refuge': some hear the cities of refuge of Numbers 35.
b: The verb katapheugō means to flee to a place of safety. (1) Some readers hear the cities of refuge, where a person who had killed by accident could run and be safe (Numbers 35:11; Deuteronomy 19:1-10); notably, the refugee could go home when the high priest died (Numbers 35:25-28). (2) Others think of fleeing to an altar for sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50). (3) Others take it simply as running to God. The 'hope that lies ahead of us' is like the 'race that lies ahead' in 12:1, the same verb.

p: An anchor holds a ship steady in a storm. This one is fixed not on the sea floor but in heaven.
b: The image is unusual: an anchor goes down, but this one goes in, 'to the inner side of the veil'. Hope, for Hebrews, is not wishful thinking but a firm line fastened to something solid that you cannot see, Christ in God's presence. 'Soul' (psychē) here means the whole self, the life.

a: the inner side of the veil
p: The very words of Leviticus 16: the place the high priest entered once a year.
b: The Greek to esōteron tou katapetasmatos, 'the inside of the veil', is the phrase of Leviticus 16:2 and 16:12 in the Greek, where God tells Aaron not to come 'inside the veil' at any time he likes, only on the Day of Atonement with blood and incense. The veil (katapetasma) hung between the holy place and the most holy place (Exodus 26:33). Hebrews returns to it at 9:3 and 10:20. The Gospels tell how it was torn when Jesus died (Mark 15:38; Matthew 27:51).
r: Leviticus 16:2; Leviticus 16:12; Exodus 26:33; Hebrews 9:3; Hebrews 10:20; Mark 15:38

p: Prodromos: a runner sent ahead, a scout. The high priest went in alone; this one goes ahead of others.
b: Prodromos was used of advance troops, scouts and runners who went ahead to prepare the way. The point is that others will follow: the Levitical high priest went behind the veil alone and came out again, but Jesus has gone in 'for us' so that we may come in after him (10:19-20). It fits the 'Founder' who leads many sons to glory (2:10).

a: Melchizedek was Salem's king and a priest of God Most High
p: Hebrews retells Genesis 14:17-20, where Melchizedek appears for three verses and is gone.
b: The site's Genesis reads: "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was a priest of God Most High." (Genesis 14:18). He blesses Abram, and "Abram gave him a tenth of everything." (Genesis 14:20). He is mentioned only once more in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 110:4. Hebrews builds its argument on everything Genesis says about him, and on everything it does not say (7:3). Hebrews does not mention the bread and wine, which many Christians later read as a picture of the Lord's Supper.

p: Salem is an old name for Jerusalem, as Psalm 76:2 shows.
b: The site's Psalm sets the names in parallel: "His lair was in Salem, / and his den in Zion." (Psalm 76:2). The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 14:18 calls him 'the king of Jerusalem'. That matters for Psalm 110: the king of David's line in Jerusalem inherits the city's ancient priest-king tradition. Hebrews does not argue from geography; it reads the name: 'Salem' sounds like shalom, 'peace' (7:2).

p: Malki-tsedeq means 'king of righteousness' (or 'my king is righteous'); Salem sounds like shalom, 'peace'.
b: In Hebrew malki-tsedeq joins melekh, 'king', and tsedeq, 'righteousness'. Shalem is close to shalom, 'peace'. Philo of Alexandria read the names the same way: he calls Melchizedek 'the king of peace, that is of Salem' and 'a just king'. For Hebrews the order matters: righteousness first, then peace, as in Psalm 85:10 and Isaiah 32:17. Hebrews uses names as signs, as Jewish interpreters did.

a: He has no father, no mother, no family tree
p: A man who pictures Christ, a heavenly being, Christ himself, or Shem son of Noah: readers have said all four.
b: (1) A human king whose parents Genesis does not mention. Hebrews argues from that silence: what Scripture leaves out makes him a picture of an eternal priest. This is the most common Christian reading of Hebrews, though some scholars hear an angelic figure behind it. (2) A heavenly being, the angelic figure of some Jewish texts. The Dead Sea text 11QMelchizedek, usually dated to about 100 BC, makes Melchizedek a heavenly figure who frees captives, brings atonement and judges with God. (3) Christ himself, appearing before his birth: a view some Christians held, though 7:3 says he was 'made like' the Son, not that he was the Son. (4) Shem son of Noah: so the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 14:18 and the Talmud (Bavli Nedarim 32b). 2 Enoch 69-73, whose date is uncertain, tells of a Melchizedek born without a father and taken to paradise.

a: He has been made like the Son of God
p: The order matters: Melchizedek is modeled on the Son, not the other way around.
b: Aphōmoiōmenos means 'made to resemble'. Hebrews does not say Christ is a copy of Melchizedek. It says Melchizedek, as Genesis portrays him, was shaped as a likeness of the Son, the true eternal priest. This is the way Hebrews reads the Old Testament throughout: the earlier figures are shadows, Christ is the reality (8:5; 10:1).
orig: ἀφωμοιωμένος δὲ τῷ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ

p: Eis to diēnekes, 'without a break': a different phrase from 'forever' (eis ton aiōna).
b: Hebrews has two phrases. Eis ton aiōna, 'forever', comes from Psalm 110:4. Eis to diēnekes, 'continually, for all time, without interruption', is its own; it comes back in 10:1 (sacrifices offered on and on), 10:12 (one sacrifice for all time) and 10:14 (made perfect for all time). The Plain renders this one 'for all time'. Melchizedek 'remains a priest' in the sense that Scripture never records an end to his priesthood.

p: Akrothinia: the top of the heap, the best of the spoils of war.
b: Akrothinion is from akros, 'top', and this, 'heap': the top of the pile, the choicest part of the plunder, the part one would give to a god. Genesis says simply 'a tenth of everything' (14:20). Hebrews stresses Abraham's dignity, 'the patriarch himself', to make Melchizedek greater still.

a: take a tenth from the people
p: In Numbers 18 the Levites receive the tithe, and the priests a tenth of that. Hebrews compresses this.
b: The law gave the tithe to the Levites: "To the descendants of Levi, look, I give every tithe in Israel as an inheritance" (Numbers 18:21). The Levites then gave "a tenth of the tithe" (Numbers 18:26) to the priests. Hebrews speaks of 'those of Levi's sons who take up the priesthood', meaning the whole tribe in its service, as Nehemiah 10:37-38 has priests present when the Levites collect. The point stands: Levi's family took tithes from their own brothers, but Melchizedek, from outside the family, took a tithe from Abraham himself.

p: The Greek says 'loins', the Hebrew way of speaking of descent. 7:10 uses the same picture.
b: Osphys is 'loins, hip', the seat of strength and of fathering children in biblical idiom (Genesis 35:11, 'kings will come out of your loins'). The Plain says 'body'. The image sets up 7:9-10: Levi was 'still in his father's body' when Abraham paid the tithe.
orig: ἐκ τῆς ὀσφύος Ἀβραάμ (ek tēs osphyos Abraam)

a: one about whom the witness is given that he is alive
p: Genesis records no death for Melchizedek. Hebrews reads that silence as a witness.
b: (1) Most read it as the argument from silence of 7:3: Scripture tells of no death, so in the story he 'lives', a figure of a priest who does not die. (2) Some see more: that Melchizedek was a heavenly being still alive (compare 11QMelchizedek). (3) Others think the witness is Psalm 110:4, 'a priest forever', which Hebrews has just quoted. In 7:16 and 7:25 the point is made of Christ himself, who lives by 'the power of a life that can never be torn down'.

t: A writer who knows it is a stretch
p: Hōs epos eipein, 'so to speak': a classical idiom found nowhere else in the New Testament.
b: The phrase is polished literary Greek, used when a speaker knows he is putting something in a bold or unusual way. The writer admits that Levi paying tithes through Abraham is a figure of speech. Even so, the idea that an ancestor carries his descendants within him was familiar: Genesis 25:23 speaks of two nations in Rebekah's womb, and Paul says all died 'in Adam' (1 Corinthians 15:22).

p: Teleiōsis: completion, reaching the goal. The Levitical system could not bring people there.
b: Teleiōsis belongs to the 'perfect' family (2:10; 5:9, 14; 6:1). In the Greek of Leviticus it was also a word for the ordination of priests (Leviticus 8:33, 'the days of your ordination'). Hebrews' claim is that the old priesthood could not bring worshipers to the goal, a clean conscience and free access to God (9:9; 10:1, 14). 7:19 says it outright: the law did not make anything perfect.

a: the priesthood on which the people's law was based
p: Greek: 'on the basis of it the people had been given law'. The law and the priesthood stand or fall together.
b: Ho laos gar ep' autēs nenomothetētai can mean 'the people received the law on the basis of it' or 'about it'. Much of the law of Moses is about priests, sacrifices and the tent, and the people's life with God depended on that priesthood working. So Hebrews draws a bold conclusion in 7:12: if God promises a new priest of another kind, the law itself must change.
orig: ὁ λαὸς γὰρ ἐπ᾽ αὐτῆς νενομοθέτηται

p: One of the strongest lines in the New Testament about the law of Moses. Jews and Christians read it differently.
b: Hebrews says that when the priesthood moves, 'a change of law' (nomou metathesis) must follow. Christians have understood the change in different ways: the whole law of Moses as a covenant ends in Christ; its priestly and sacrificial rules end while its moral commands remain; or it is not abolished but fulfilled and transformed. Jewish readers answer that the Torah gives Aaron's sons "a priesthood for all time" (Exodus 40:15), and that Judaism kept faith after the Temple fell: when Rabbi Joshua mourned the ruined Temple, 'the place where atonement was made', Rabban Johanan ben Zakkai answered, 'we have another means of atonement which is as effective, and that is, the practice of lovingkindness', citing Hosea 6:6 (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 4). Hebrews' own claim here is narrower: the law of priesthood by descent from Levi has given way to a priest of Judah. See 8:13 on 'old' and the book page on Hebrews and the Jewish people.
r: Exodus 40:15; Hosea 6:6; Matthew 5:17-18; Romans 10:4; Galatians 3:24-25; Hebrews 8:13; Hebrews 10:9

p: Anatellō is the verb of the sun rising and of a plant springing up: both were messianic pictures.
b: Anatetalken, 'has risen, sprung up'. In the Greek of Numbers 24:17 Balaam says 'a star will rise (anatelei) out of Jacob', and the Greek of Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 6:12 call the coming Branch anatolē, 'rising, sprouting'. So the word may carry a messianic overtone. The plain fact Hebrews relies on is that Jesus was of the tribe of Judah, the royal tribe of David (Matthew 1:1-3; Romans 1:3; Revelation 5:5), not of Levi.
orig: ἐξ Ἰούδα ἀνατέταλκεν ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν
r: Numbers 24:17; Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 6:12; Luke 1:78; Revelation 5:5; Romans 1:3

a: a law with a command about the flesh
p: Sarkinēs, 'made of flesh': the old priesthood passed by bodily descent.
b: The critical text reads sarkinēs, 'made of flesh' (the site's term); the Byzantine text has sarkikēs, 'fleshly', with no real change of sense. The 'command about the flesh' is the rule that priests must be born into Aaron's family. Christ's priesthood rests instead on 'the power of a life that can never be torn down' (akatalytou, 'indissoluble'): the resurrection life, which death could not undo.

p: Athetēsis, a legal word for declaring a document void. 9:26 uses it for doing away with sin.
b: Athetēsis means setting aside, annulling, as one would void a document. The 'command that came before' is the law of priestly descent; it is set aside 'because it was weak and did no good', not because it was evil, but because it could not bring people to the goal (7:19). Hebrews uses the same word at 9:26: Christ appeared 'to cancel sin'.

p: Under the law only the priests came near. In Christ all God's people do.
b: The verb here is engizō, 'draw near', close to 'come near' (proserchomai) of 4:16 and 7:25. In the law, coming near to God at the altar was the priests' privilege; a layman who came near could die (Numbers 18:7). The 'better hope' brings every believer near. James 4:8 uses the same verb: 'Come near to God, and he will come near to you.'

a: The Lord has taken an oath, and he will not go back on it
p: The first half of Psalm 110:4, which 5:6 and 7:17 left out: God swore it.
b: The site's Psalm reads: "The LORD has taken an oath, and he will not go back on it:" (Psalm 110:4). Hebrews has 'the Lord' because the Greek has no divine name. Aaron's sons became priests by birth, with no oath; this priest was installed by God's oath, which God will not take back. Hebrews has already taught that God's oath makes a promise unchangeable (6:16-18).

a: the one who guarantees a better covenant
p: Engyos: a surety, someone who puts himself up as bail. This is the first time Hebrews says 'covenant'.
b: Engyos, found only here in the New Testament, was the legal word for a surety: a person who guarantees that a debt will be paid or a promise kept, at his own cost. Jesus stands surety for the new covenant: his life guarantees that it will hold. This is also Hebrews' first use of diathēkē, 'covenant', which becomes the theme of chapters 8-10 (Jeremiah 31:31-34, quoted in Hebrews 8:8-12). For the readings at 9:16-17, see the note there.

p: Aparabaton can mean 'permanent' or 'not handed on to a successor'. Both fit.
b: Aparabatos can mean 'unchangeable, inviolable'. Some read it here as 'not transferable': unlike the Levitical priests, who died and passed their office to sons (7:23), Christ has no successor because he never dies. The Plain gives that sense; the two meanings come to the same thing.

p: Eis to panteles can mean 'completely' or 'for all time'. The Plain keeps both.
b: Eis to panteles means 'to the uttermost': completely, in every way, or for all time. Luke 13:11 uses it of a woman who could not straighten up 'at all'. Hebrews probably means both: he saves wholly, and he saves forever, because he lives forever. 'Those who come near to God through him' uses the priestly verb of 4:16.
orig: σῴζειν εἰς τὸ παντελές (sōzein eis to panteles)

p: Paul says the same of the risen Christ at God's right hand; Isaiah of the servant.
b: The verb entynchanō is the site's 'plead', as in Romans: "He is at God's right hand, and he pleads for us." (Romans 8:34). 1 John 2:1 calls Jesus 'an Advocate with the Father'. The servant of Isaiah 53 'will step in for the rebels' (Isaiah 53:12). Christians differ over what the pleading means: a continual prayer, or the simple fact that the crucified one is present before God, his finished sacrifice speaking for us (12:24).

a: holy, free of evil, free of stain
p: The law demanded a high priest without defect and kept from defilement. Christ is pure in himself.
b: Leviticus 21 sets strict rules for the high priest: he must not touch a dead body, even of his parents, and must keep himself from defilement (Leviticus 21:10-15). Hebrews' list goes deeper: hosios (holy, devoted to God), akakos (without evil), amiantos (undefiled), 'separated from sinners' (not by avoiding them but by being without sin, 4:15), and exalted above the heavens. 13:4 uses amiantos of the marriage bed.

p: Leviticus has the high priest offer for himself and the people yearly, on the Day of Atonement. Why 'each day'?
b: Leviticus 16 has the high priest offer first for himself and then for the people once a year. Readers explain 'each day' in several ways. (1) The high priest also had a daily offering: "This is the offering that Aaron and his sons are to present to the LORD on the day he is anointed. It is a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half in the morning and half in the evening." (Leviticus 6:20). (2) Hebrews is joining the daily sacrifices of the priests (10:11) to the yearly sacrifice of the high priest, as one system that never ended. (3) 'Each day' goes with 'need': every day the priests stood in need of offering again. All agree on the contrast: Christ offered once for all.

p: Ephapax: once, never to be repeated. A key word for Christ's sacrifice in Hebrews.
b: Ephapax means 'once and for all time'. Hebrews uses it of Christ's offering here, at 9:12 (he entered the sanctuary once for all) and 10:10 (we have been made holy through the offering of his body, once for all); the simpler hapax, 'once', comes in 9:26-28. Paul uses ephapax in Romans 6:10: he died to sin once for all. How this 'once for all' relates to the Eucharist is a question on which churches differ: see the traditions card on Hebrews 10.

a: by bringing himself up as the offering
p: Anapherō: 'bring up' onto the altar. Here the priest brings up himself.
b: Anapherō, 'carry up', is the verb for putting a sacrifice up on the altar (Leviticus 14:20 Greek; James 2:21, Abraham 'offering up' Isaac). The startling thing is the object: 'himself'. In the old system priest and victim were always different. Here they are the same person, which is why the offering was enough, once. 9:14 says he 'offered himself flawless to God through the eternal Spirit'.

t: The last words of the argument
p: The section ends with three of Hebrews' key words: Son, perfect, forever.
b: The Greek ends huion eis ton aiōna teteleiōmenon, 'a Son, forever made perfect'. 'Son' takes us back to 1:2 and 5:5; 'made perfect' to 2:10 and 5:9; 'forever' to Psalm 110:4. The law appointed weak men; God's oath, which came after the law (Psalm 110 was written long after Sinai), appointed the Son. 8:1 will sum up: 'the high priest we have is of that kind'.
